questions.question: What is the JavaScript event loop and how does it work?
questions.title: Event Loop Basics
questions.direct_answer: The runtime processes the call stack synchronously; when it's empty, microtasks (Promises) drain, then macrotasks (setTimeout, I/O) run one at a time. microtask → macrotask priority; async never runs while the stack is busy.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: The runtime processes the call stack synchronously; when it's empty, microtasks (Promises) drain, then macrotasks (setTimeout, I/O) run one at a time. microtask → macrotask priority; async never runs while the stack is busy.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S[call stack] -->|empty?| LOOP{event loop}
    LOOP --> MT{microtask queue?}
    MT -->|non-empty| M[drain ALL microtasks]
    M --> MT
    MT -->|empty| T[run ONE macrotask]
    T --> S
    SYNC[synchronous code] -->|blocks| S
    HOST[async I/O / setTimeout] →|callback done| Q[queued]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The loop's precise steps (per the HTML spec's event-loop processing model): (1) pick the oldest task from the task queue; (2) run it; (3) drain the ENTIRE microtask queue; (4) render if needed; (5) repeat. The key asymmetry: one macrotask per iteration, but ALL microtasks drain — that's the priority guarantee.

The async operation's path (where the concurrency actually lives): fetch/setTimeout/file-read are handled by the HOST (the browser's Web APIs, Node's libuv) — NOT by the JS thread. When the async op completes, the host puts the callback in the appropriate queue. The JS thread sees only the queues — it never blocks on the operation itself.

The starvation check (the spec-level gotcha): a microtask that adds another microtask (Promise.resolve().then(function f() { Promise.resolve().then(f) })) blocks macrotasks FOREVER — the microtask queue never empties, the loop never advances to the timer queue. setTimeout callbacks starve. The spec doesn't protect against this — your code is the protection.

questions.question: How does the 'this' keyword work in JavaScript?
questions.title: This Keyword Javascript
questions.direct_answer: this is determined by HOW the function is called: method call (obj.fn()) — this = obj; plain call (fn()) — undefined/global; arrow functions — NO this of their own (inherit from creation); bind/call/apply — explicitly set.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OBJ[obj.method()] →|dot syntax| O[this = obj]
    FN[fn()] →|plain call| U[this = undefined or global]
    AR[arrow fn] →|lexical| I[inherits creation-scope this]
    CALL[fn.call obj] →|explicit| E[this = obj]
    BIND[fn.bind obj] →|permanent| P[bound forever]
    NEW[new Fn()] →|constructor| N[this = new instance]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The binding semantics' reason for the confusion (the historical context): JavaScript's this predates classes — the design was for shared methods on objects where the receiver provides the context. The rules follow from the CALL-SITE syntax (how you invoke determines what this is), which is unlike Java/C++ where this is the instance pointer bound at definition.

The arrow function's [[ThisMode]] (the spec detail for depth): arrows are created with lexical this — their [[Environment]] captures the this of the enclosing function at CREATION time. They don't just 'not have this' — they're lexically scoped TO it, exactly like closures capture outer variables. The call/apply/bind on an arrow does nothing to this (the spec defines arrows as non-bindable).

The class-method trap (the modern follow-up): class methods (not arrow fields) are PROTOTYPES — this is call-site-bound. A method extracted and passed as a callback (this.handleClick as a prop) loses this. The fixes: constructor binding, the class-fields arrow (handleClick = () => { ... } — a class field that's an arrow, bound to the instance at construction). The class-fields pattern is the React idiom.
